name: Jingdezhen — China's porcelain capital
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The 'Porcelain Capital' in Jiangxi, China, whose kilns burned for a thousand years. T1: for centuries hundreds of kilns here glowed day and night so brightly the town was said to be 'lit by fire at midnight' — Jingdezhen is called China's Porcelain Capital (invert the wonder: the fires/scale is the hook, the town's title is the answer). T2: the secret white ingredient is a clay dug from a nearby hill named Gaoling ('high ridge') — the hill's own name became the English word KAOLIN (answer = kaolin / the word comes from a hill's name). T3: the emperor kept a private 'imperial kiln' here, and only he could own porcelain painted with the five-clawed dragon. T4: the porcelain was so fine and so unmatched that Europeans named the whole material after the country it came from — 'china.' T5: in 1712 a French Jesuit priest, Père d'Entrecolles, living in Jingdezhen, wrote letters home describing the secret recipe — the leak that helped Europe finally reproduce porcelain (the town itself was renamed for Emperor Zhenzong's Jingde reign of 1004, when he ordered wares stamped with his reign-name).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaolinite (VERIFIED: 'kaolin' borrowed 1727 from d'Entrecolles' 1712 reports on Jingdezhen porcelain, from Gaoling 'High Ridge' village near Jingdezhen); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen_porcelain + /wiki/Jingdezhen (imperial kilns, Jingde-reign naming, d'Entrecolles — build should re-confirm the 1004 reign-name detail and imperial dragon-mark exclusivity). Grokipedia checked first per protocol but grokipedia.com returned HTTP 403 to the fetch tool.
framing_note: Voice: lead with the scene (a town on fire with kilns; a hill whose name you now say every day), never 'What is kaolin?' or 'What is the capital of porcelain?'. Every rung's answer is a concrete fact about THIS town or its clay. Dinner-test payoff = the 'china' = country = material naming rung (T4) and the Gaoling-became-'kaolin' rung (T2) — a kid retells both. Accuracy rail: kaolin's etymology and the d'Entrecolles leak are firmly documented; keep the five-clawed-dragon exclusivity phrased as imperial-court rule. Lane: the clay/geology sits fine in geography (a real mineral from a real hill); the recipe/craft is culture — both in-lane, no food overlap. Pairs as a distractor set with the Meissen ladder (Europe's answer to china).

name: Silk — China's two-thousand-year secret
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The guarded craft of sericulture, born in China. T1: silk is spun by a caterpillar — the silkworm (Bombyx mori) — which eats only mulberry leaves and wraps itself in a cocoon made of ONE unbroken thread up to about a kilometre long (hook = a single thread that long; answer = it's one caterpillar's cocoon). T2: Chinese legend credits Empress Leizu with discovering silk around 3000 BC when a cocoon dropped into her cup of hot tea and unravelled into a shining thread (label LEGEND). T3: China guarded the secret of making silk for roughly TWO THOUSAND years — carrying silkworm eggs out of the country could be punished by death. T4: around 552 AD the Byzantine emperor Justinian sent two monks who smuggled silkworm eggs out of China hidden inside hollow bamboo canes, finally breaking the monopoly (dinner-test payoff). T5: the overland trade in this cloth named the 'Silk Road,' the caravan network running some 6,400 km from Chang'an (today's Xi'an) to the Mediterranean.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_silk (VERIFIED: ~2000-yr guarded secret; Justinian c.552 AD sent monks who smuggled silkworm eggs in bamboo/rods; Leizu ~3000 BC cocoon-in-tea legend; Bombyx mori feeds on mulberry). Grokipedia checked first per protocol (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led — the empress's teacup, the monks' hollow staffs — never 'What is silk made of?'. Invert the wonder: the km-long thread and the death-penalty secrecy are hooks, the knowable fact is the answer. Dinner-test payoff = the two monks smuggling eggs in hollow bamboo canes (T4). Accuracy rail: label the Leizu teacup as legend; the Justinian smuggling and the ~2,000-year monopoly are the documented backbone. LANE (animal): the silkworm is a one-rung PROCESS mention (it makes the thread) — keep answers on the craft and the guarded place, never the caterpillar's biology, which belongs to the animal bank. Xi'an/Chang'an anchors the Silk Road rung as a real place.

name: The Four Great Inventions of ancient China
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: Four world-changing inventions born in China, one per rung. T1 (paper): a Han-dynasty court official, Cai Lun (around 105 AD), perfected paper from mashed bark, rag and old fishnet, replacing heavy bamboo strips (answer = paper / Cai Lun's mash). T2 (printing): the world's oldest DATED printed book is a Chinese Buddhist scroll, the Diamond Sutra of 868 AD, made by carved woodblocks centuries before Gutenberg. T3 (movable type): around 1040 a commoner named Bi Sheng carved each character in baked clay — movable type, roughly 400 years before Gutenberg's European press. T4 (compass): the first compass wasn't for sailors — Han-dynasty Chinese carved a spoon of lodestone (the 'sinan') that spun to point SOUTH, used to lay out buildings and for divination. T5 (gunpowder): Tang-dynasty alchemists mixing saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal were chasing an ELIXIR OF IMMORTALITY — and stumbled onto gunpowder (huoyao, 'fire medicine') instead (dinner-test payoff: seeking eternal life, they invented an explosive).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Great_Inventions; /wiki/Cai_Lun (~105 AD); /wiki/Diamond_Sutra (868 AD, oldest dated printed book); /wiki/Bi_Sheng (movable type ~1040); /wiki/Gunpowder (Tang alchemists / elixir of immortality). Build should re-confirm each date at author stage. Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: each rung sets a scene and the answer names WHICH invention or its ironic origin, never a bare date. Invert the wonder: the alchemists' goal (eternal life) is the payoff answer for gunpowder, not the word 'gunpowder.' Anchor = China / its dynastic courts (a real place per rung). Anti-restatement rail: the stem gives the scene (alchemists chasing immortality; a spoon that spins), the player must KNOW which invention/origin — the other three great inventions make live, adjacent distractors. Dinner-test payoff = gunpowder-from-the-immortality-elixir (T5), and the south-pointing sinan spoon (T4). No history-bank duplication if answers stay on the inventions themselves, not on later wars/print revolutions.

name: Murano — Venice's island of glass
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The lagoon island where Venice hid its glassmakers. T1: in 1291 Venice ordered ALL its glassmakers onto one small island, Murano — partly because the roaring furnaces kept setting fire to the wooden city (hook = a whole trade exiled to an island; answer = to stop the fires / and guard the secret). T2: the deeper reason was secrecy — a Murano glassmaker was forbidden to leave Venice, and betraying the craft's secrets could be punished by DEATH (dinner-test payoff). T3: yet the glassmakers were treated almost as nobles — a glassmaker's daughter could marry into a noble family without her children losing rank. T4: in the 1400s Angelo Barovier invented 'cristallo' — glass so clear it looked like carved rock crystal, then the finest in the world. T5: Murano's 'millefiori' ('thousand flowers') fuses bundles of colored glass rods so that every slice reveals a tiny flower hidden inside the glass.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murano_glass (VERIFIED: 1291 law confining glassmaking to Murano for fire-risk + secrecy; leaving/revealing secrets punishable by death; cristallo by Angelo Barovier, 15th c.; millefiori = 'thousand flowers'; 1376 privilege that a glassmaker's daughter marrying a noble kept noble rank). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: lead with the scene (a burning city; craftsmen who could never leave), never 'What is Murano glass?'. Each answer is a concrete fact about THIS island's craft. Dinner-test payoff = glassmakers forbidden to leave on pain of death (T2), with the daughter-marries-a-noble privilege (T3) as the surprising twist. Accuracy rail: the 1291 date, the death-penalty secrecy, and Barovier's cristallo are documented — keep them precise. Distractors stay adjacent-but-real: Bohemian/Czech crystal, Venetian mirrors, Tiffany glass. No lane conflicts.

name: Persian carpets — Iran's woven gardens
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The knotted carpets of Iran. T1: a fine Persian carpet packs hundreds of hand-tied knots into a single square inch — the famous Ardabil Carpet holds about 26 MILLION knots in one rug (hook = the knot count; answer = it's all tied by hand, one knot at a time). T2: the Ardabil Carpet (made 1539-40) is signed by its weaver, Maqsud of Kashan, carries a couplet by the poet Hafez, and today hangs in the V&A museum in London. T3: Persian weavers use the asymmetric 'Persian knot,' which lets them bend fine curving flower-and-vine designs that blockier knots can't. T4: many are 'garden carpets' — a walled paradise garden with water channels, seen from above — and the Old Persian word for such a walled garden, 'pairidaeza,' is where we get the word PARADISE (dinner-test payoff). T5: rival weaving cities each have a signature style — Tabriz, Isfahan, Kashan, Kerman — readable by pattern and palette (optional labeled-LEGEND rung: some weavers left one deliberate flaw, saying only God is perfect — a tradition, not a rule).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardabil_Carpet (VERIFIED: ~26 million knots; 300-350 knots/sq inch; made 946 AH = 1539-40; signed Maqsud of Kashan; Hafez couplet; larger carpet at the V&A, London); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_carpet (VERIFIED: asymmetric Persian knot; Tabriz/Isfahan/Kashan/Kerman centers; garden carpets). 'Paradise' from Old Persian pairidaeza — well-established etymology (build cite en.wiktionary/paradise). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led — a rug that is 26 million knots, a woven garden you look down into — never 'What is a Persian carpet?'. Dinner-test payoff = pairidaeza-gave-us-'paradise' (T4), with the 26-million-knots hook (T1). Accuracy rail: the deliberate-flaw idea is FOLKLORE/DISPUTED — if used, label it a tradition weavers sometimes spoke of, never state it as a rule. Keep the Ardabil facts exact (date, weaver, V&A). Distractors = other real rug traditions (Turkish/Anatolian Ghiordes-knot rugs, Turkmen, Kashmiri). No lane conflicts.

name: Damascus steel — the lost watered blades
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The legendary patterned swords sold in Damascus. T1: a true Damascus blade carried a rippling, flowing pattern locked into the metal, like water frozen in steel (hook = the water-pattern; answer = it's IN the steel, not painted on). T2: despite the name, the steel came as 'wootz' ingots from India and Sri Lanka — smiths in Damascus, Syria forged and sold them (the Arabic 'damas' also means 'watered'). T3: legends said a real blade could slice a silk scarf drifting down onto its edge, and cut clean through lesser swords (label LEGEND). T4: the craft was LOST — by around 1900 no living smith could make it, and even now the exact wootz method is only partly reverse-engineered (dinner-test payoff: a technology humans forgot how to do). T5: in 2006 scientists reported carbon nanotubes and cementite bands inside an antique blade — a possible clue to its edge, though experts still argue about it (label DISPUTED).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus_steel (VERIFIED: high-carbon crucible/wootz steel from southern India + Sri Lanka, forged/sold in Damascus; 'damas' = watered; name likely early branding; production ceased ~1900, last account 1903; 2006 German report of nanotubes/cementite, disputed; legends of cutting silk and iron). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: lead with the blade and its water-pattern, never 'What is Damascus steel?'. Dinner-test payoff = the lost-and-only-half-recovered craft (T4). CRITICAL accuracy rail: the 'Damascus' name is essentially branding — the STEEL came from India/Sri Lanka (wootz); T2 must make that clear so no kid learns it was mined in Syria. Label the silk-scarf sharpness stories LEGEND and the nanotube finding DISPUTED — do NOT state either as settled fact. Distractors = other real famed steels/blade-cities (Toledo, Sheffield, Japanese tamahagane) — adjacent and wrong, never joke options.

name: Kente — the Ashanti cloth of Ghana
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The bright royal cloth of the Ashanti, born in Ghana. T1: kente is hand-woven in narrow strips on a loom in the village of Bonwire, in Ghana's Ashanti Region, then the strips are sewn edge-to-edge into a wide, dazzling cloth (place anchor = Bonwire). T2: Ashanti legend says weavers first learned the craft by watching Anansi the spider spin its web (label LEGEND; dinner-test payoff — a spider taught people to weave). T3: the name is linked to the Akan word for 'basket' (kenten), because the tight woven pattern looks basket-like. T4: every color and pattern carries a meaning — gold for royalty and wealth, blue for peace — and each design has its own name and proverb. T5: kente was once reserved for Ashanti kings and chiefs, worn draped toga-style; in the 1900s it became a worldwide symbol of African heritage.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente_cloth (VERIFIED: originates from Bonwire, Ashanti Region, Ghana; Anansi-the-spider origin story; name tied to Akan 'basket'; hand-woven silk/cotton strips; symbolic colors — gold=royalty/wealth, blue=peace; worn toga-style, royal patronage). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led — the loom in Bonwire, a spider spinning — never 'What is kente?'. Dinner-test payoff = Anansi the spider taught the first weavers (T2). Accuracy rail: label the Anansi origin a LEGEND, and keep the weavers generic (oral tradition doesn't reliably fix individual names) — don't assert named craftsmen as history. Distractors = other real African/strip textiles (mudcloth/bogolan of Mali, adire of the Yoruba, aso-oke). Respectful, celebratory tone; this is settled cultural wonder, not a stance rung. Lane: pure textile craft, no food/animal overlap.

name: Batik — Java's wax-drawn cloth
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The wax-resist dyeing of Java, Indonesia. T1: on the island of Java, artists draw on cloth with hot wax so the waxed lines RESIST the dye — when the wax is later boiled off, the hidden pattern appears (hook = drawing in wax; answer = the wax blocks the dye). T2: the wax 'pen' is the canting — a tiny copper cup with a spout on a handle that lets the artist trail wax in fine dots and lines by hand (batik tulis). T3: to make cloth faster, a carved copper stamp called a 'cap' presses the wax pattern on in one go (batik cap). T4: in the royal courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta, certain 'forbidden' patterns (larangan) — like the diagonal 'parang' — could be worn only by the sultan's family (dinner-test payoff: a pattern you could be forbidden to wear). T5: in 2009 UNESCO named Indonesian batik a Masterpiece of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batik (VERIFIED: highly developed on Java, Indonesia; wax-resist process; canting = copper reservoir/spout pen; cap = carved copper stamp; UNESCO recognition 2 Oct 2009; some patterns restricted to certain occasions). Court larangan/parang exclusivity (Yogyakarta/Surakarta) well-documented — build re-cite. Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: lead with the craft-scene (trailing hot wax, then the pattern surfacing from the dye), never 'What is batik?'. Dinner-test payoff = the forbidden royal 'parang' pattern only the sultan's family could wear (T4). Accuracy rail: keep the wax-RESIST mechanism correct (wax blocks dye — it's not painting the color on); phrase the larangan restriction as a court tradition of Yogyakarta/Surakarta. Distractors = other real resist/dye textiles (Indian bandhani tie-dye, Japanese shibori, West African adire). Lane: pure textile craft.

name: Harris Tweed — the cloth protected by law
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The hand-woven wool of Scotland's Outer Hebrides. T1: on the windswept Outer Hebrides islands — Lewis, Harris, the Uists, Barra — Harris Tweed is still hand-woven by islanders in their OWN HOMES on foot-powered treadle looms, not in a factory (hook = a world-famous cloth made in cottages; answer = handwoven at home in the Hebrides). T2: real Harris Tweed carries a stamped 'Orb' mark, a trademark since 1909, certifying each length is genuine. T3: it is protected by its very own UK Act of Parliament — the Harris Tweed Act 1993 — which legally DEFINES it: pure virgin wool, dyed and spun in the Outer Hebrides, and handwoven at the weaver's home (dinner-test payoff: a cloth with its own law). T4: the tweed was built for its place — dense, weatherproof wool made to shed Hebridean wind and rain, its muted colors once drawn from local plants and lichens.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harris_Tweed (VERIFIED: made in the Outer Hebrides — Lewis/Harris/Uists/Benbecula/Barra; handwoven on a treadle loom at each weaver's home; the Orb trademark granted 1909; Harris Tweed Act 1993 statutory definition — pure virgin wool dyed/spun in the Outer Hebrides, handwoven at home). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led — a global luxury cloth still woven in island cottages — never 'What is Harris Tweed?'. Dinner-test payoff = it's protected by its OWN Act of Parliament (T3). Accuracy rail: do NOT over-claim it's 'the only fabric with its own law' (widely repeated but not confirmed) — phrase it as 'its own Act of Parliament, the Harris Tweed Act 1993.' Place-anchor every rung to the Outer Hebrides. Distractors = other named regional cloths (Donegal tweed, Shetland wool, cashmere). Lane: textile craft; the sheep are a one-word source mention, not animal-bank biology.

name: Ryoan-ji — Kyoto's garden of stone
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The Zen dry-landscape garden in Kyoto, Japan. T1: at the Ryoan-ji temple in Kyoto sits a famous 'dry garden' (karesansui) with NO plants and NO water — just a rectangle of raked white gravel and 15 bare stones (hook = a garden with nothing growing; answer = a dry/Zen rock garden). T2: the white gravel is combed daily into straight lines and rings, meant to suggest rippling water or the sea flowing around islands. T3: the 15 stones are set so cleverly that from anywhere on the viewing veranda you can see at most 14 — one stone is ALWAYS hidden behind another, no matter where you stand (dinner-test payoff). T4: the garden isn't made to walk through — it's a puzzle you sit and contemplate, a place for Zen meditation.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ry%C5%8Dan-ji (VERIFIED: Kyoto; karesansui dry-landscape garden; 15 stones; from the veranda at least one stone is always hidden — you can never see all 15 at once; raked gravel; late-15th-century origin; UNESCO World Heritage). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: lead with the strangeness (a garden with nothing planted; gravel raked like water), never 'What is a Zen garden?' — teach the term 'karesansui' in the rung before testing it. Dinner-test payoff = you can never see all 15 stones at once, one is always hidden (T3) — the single most retellable fact. Accuracy rail: the 'always at least one hidden' fact is real and specific — keep it exact (at most 14 visible). Anchor every rung to Ryoan-ji / Kyoto. Distractors = other real Japanese garden types (stroll garden, tea garden, moss garden). Pairs thematically with the kintsugi mini as Japanese aesthetics.

name: Tartan and the kilt — Highland Scotland
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The clan cloth of the Scottish Highlands. T1: in the Scottish Highlands the tartan is a criss-cross woven pattern (its repeating unit is called the 'sett'), and the original 'great kilt' was one long belted plaid wrapped around the whole body (hook = one cloth, worn as a whole outfit; answer = the great kilt / belted plaid). T2: after the Jacobites were crushed at Culloden in 1746, Britain's Dress Act BANNED the kilt and tartan in the Highlands — you could be jailed, or shipped overseas, for wearing your own clan's cloth (dinner-test payoff: a clothing pattern made illegal). T3: the ban was lifted in 1782 and tartan came roaring back — but much of the tidy 'one clan, one tartan' idea was actually a romantic invention of the 1800s, not ancient law. T4: today an official Scottish Register of Tartans records thousands of named setts, from clans to districts to companies.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dress_Act_1746 (VERIFIED: part of the Act of Proscription after the 1745 Jacobite rising / Battle of Culloden; banned the plaid, philabeg/little kilt and tartan north of the Highland line; repealed by the Use of Highland Dress Act 1782). Sett/great-kilt and the 19th-c. clan-tartan romanticization + Scottish Register of Tartans — build re-cite. Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led — a cloth so tied to identity that a government outlawed it — never 'What is tartan?'. Dinner-test payoff = the kilt/tartan was banned by law after Culloden (T2). Accuracy rail: be honest that much clan-specific tartan is a 19th-century romantic invention (Sir Walter Scott / George IV's 1822 visit), NOT ancient — don't feed the myth. HISTORY-LANE BORDER: Culloden and the 1745 Jacobite rising are a military/dynastic episode the history bank may own — keep EVERY rung's answer on the CLOTH (the sett, the great kilt, the clothing ban and its 1782 repeal, the tartan register), never on the battle's course or the Jacobite cause. Distractors = other real regional patterns/garments.
history_overlap: The Dress Act rung touches the aftermath of the Battle of Culloden / the 1745 Jacobite rising, which the history bank may cover as a military-dynastic episode. Keep answers on the clothing and its ban/repeal, not the battle itself, to avoid duplicating a history ladder.

name: Cremona — the town of Stradivarius violins
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The Italian town that built the world's finest violins. T1: in the small Italian town of Cremona, around the year 1700, Antonio Stradivari made violins now considered the greatest ever built — a 'Stradivarius' (place anchor = Cremona; answer = the violin/its maker). T2: of the roughly 1,100 instruments Stradivari built, about 650 survive, and single violins now sell for millions of dollars. T3: his 'golden period' (about 1700-1720) instruments are the most prized; one, 'the Messiah' of 1716, was kept so pristine it has barely ever been played and now sits in Oxford's Ashmolean Museum. T4: one theory for the magic sound: the 'Little Ice Age' (about 1645-1750) made trees grow slowly and evenly, giving unusually DENSE Alpine spruce for the wood. T5: yet in blind listening tests, expert players often can't reliably tell a Stradivarius from a fine modern violin — the 'secret' has never actually been proven (dinner-test payoff: maybe the legend beats the science).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stradivarius (VERIFIED: made in Cremona by Antonio Stradivari, late-17th/early-18th c.; ~650 of >1,100 survive; golden period ~1700-1725; Little Ice Age / dense-wood theory ~1645-1750; blind tests find no reliable sound difference vs modern violins). 'The Messiah' (1716, Ashmolean, Oxford, nearly unplayed) — build cite en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messiah_Stradivarius. Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: lead with the town and the mystery, never 'What is a Stradivarius?'. Dinner-test payoff = the honest twist that blind tests can't reliably pick out a Strad (T5) — teaches HOW WE KNOW, not just awe. Accuracy rail: present the sound 'secret' as competing THEORIES, not proven fact; the Little Ice Age wood idea and the blind-test result are both real and both belong. Keep 'the Messiah / Ashmolean' precise. Distractors = other real Cremona makers/instruments (Guarneri 'del Gesù', Amati, Guadagnini) and other craft-towns. No lane conflict.

name: Meissen — how Europe cracked China's porcelain secret
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The Saxon town where Europe first made true porcelain. T1: in the town of Meissen in Saxony, Germany, Europe finally made its first true hard-paste porcelain in 1710 — matching Chinese 'china' at last after centuries of failing (place anchor = Meissen). T2: the breakthrough came from Johann Friedrich Böttger, an alchemist LOCKED UP by Augustus the Strong, who demanded Böttger turn cheap metal into GOLD (dinner-test payoff: imprisoned to make gold). T3: Böttger never made a speck of gold — but working with the scientist Tschirnhaus he cracked the porcelain recipe (kaolin was the missing key), and porcelain became known as 'white gold.' T4: Meissen's crossed-swords mark, added in 1720, is one of the oldest trademarks still in use today.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissen_porcelain (VERIFIED: first European hard-paste porcelain; Böttger held in 'protective custody' by Augustus II 'the Strong' to make gold; worked with Tschirnhaus; kaolin the vital ingredient; production started 1710 at Albrechtsburg, Meissen; crossed-swords mark introduced 1720, one of the oldest trademarks). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led — an alchemist jailed to make gold who instead makes 'white gold' — never 'What is Meissen porcelain?'. Dinner-test payoff = Böttger imprisoned to transmute gold, cracks porcelain instead (T2). Accuracy rail: keep the story precise — Böttger did NOT make gold; kaolin was the key; 1710 first production, 1720 crossed-swords mark. Deliberately pairs with the Jingdezhen ladder (the secret China guarded; the secret Europe stole) — distractors = rival European porcelain towns (Delft, Sèvres, Limoges, Wedgwood). No lane conflict.

name: The didgeridoo — Arnhem Land, Australia
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: One of the world's oldest wind instruments, from northern Australia. T1: in Arnhem Land in northern Australia, Aboriginal people play the didgeridoo — a long wooden drone-pipe, among the world's oldest wind instruments (hook = a pipe that plays one endless humming note; answer = the didgeridoo). T2: it's not carved hollow by hand — makers search out eucalyptus branches that TERMITES have eaten hollow from the inside, then cut and trim them (dinner-test payoff: insects make the instrument). T3: players use 'circular breathing' — breathing IN through the nose while pushing stored air out with puffed cheeks — to hold one note without a break for minutes on end. T4: the Yolngu people of northeast Arnhem Land call it the 'yidaki'; rock paintings show it's been played for well over a thousand years (accuracy rail: NOT the popular '40,000 years' claim).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didgeridoo (VERIFIED: developed by Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia, Arnhem Land; made from eucalyptus hollowed by termites; circular breathing = inhale through nose while expelling stored air via cheeks; Yolngu name 'yidaki'; archaeology/rock art suggests use for LESS THAN ~1,000 years in Kakadu, a ~1,500-year-old rock painting shows a player — the '40,000 years / oldest instrument' claim is NOT supported). Grokipedia checked first (403 to fetch tool).
framing_note: Voice: lead with the sound and the place (a droning pipe from Arnhem Land), never 'What is a didgeridoo?'. Dinner-test payoff = termites hollow it out (T2), with circular breathing (T3) close behind. CRITICAL accuracy rail: correct the romantic overclaim — say 'one of the oldest' wind instruments and cite rock art of ~1,500 years, NOT '40,000 years' or 'the oldest'. Respectful tone; teach 'yidaki' as the Yolngu name. LANE (animal): the termite is a one-rung PROCESS mention (it hollows the wood) — keep the answer on the instrument, never termite biology, which is the animal bank's.

name: Kintsugi — Japan's golden mending
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The Japanese art of repairing pottery with gold. T1: in Japan, 'kintsugi' ('golden joinery') mends a broken bowl by filling the cracks with lacquer dusted with gold — so the mended seams SHINE instead of hiding (hook = a repair you're meant to see; answer = the cracks are filled with gold). T2: the idea flips how we think about damage: a bowl's break becomes part of its story and the gold-veined repair makes it MORE beautiful and more valued, not less (the wabi-sabi love of imperfection; dinner-test payoff). T3 (legend): one story says a 15th-century shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimasa, sent a cracked tea bowl to China and got it back stapled with ugly metal — so Japanese craftsmen invented a lovelier way to mend (label LEGEND).

name: The theremin — Russia's untouchable instrument
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The instrument you play without touching, invented in Russia. T1: in Russia in 1920, the physicist Leon Theremin invented an instrument you play WITHOUT EVER TOUCHING it — the theremin, that eerie wavering wail heard in old sci-fi and horror films (hook = music from thin air; answer = the theremin). T2: it has two antennas — move one hand near the upright rod to change the PITCH, the other hand near the loop to change the VOLUME — your hands sense the electric field but never make contact. T3: the same inventor later built 'The Thing,' a hidden bug with NO batteries and no wires that let the Soviets secretly listen inside the US ambassador's office for years (dinner-test payoff: the music inventor built a spy device).

name: The Panama hat — actually from Ecuador
strand: Crafts & inventions tied to a place
scope: The famous hat named after the wrong country. T1: the 'Panama hat' isn't from Panama at all — it's hand-woven in ECUADOR, in towns like Montecristi and Cuenca, from the straw of the toquilla palm (hook = a hat named after the wrong place; answer = it's really Ecuadorian). T2: it got the wrong name because the hats were SHIPPED through Panama, and President Theodore Roosevelt was photographed wearing one at the Panama Canal in 1906 — so the world credited Panama (dinner-test payoff: named for its shipping port, not its home). T3: the finest 'Montecristi superfino' is woven so tightly and finely that it can hold water and be rolled up small enough to pass through a wedding ring.
